title.rendered: AKTU MBA 3rd Sem Supply Chain And Logistics Management PYQs

content.rendered:
Supply Chain And Logistics Management is an important Operation Management specialization subject in AKTU MBA 3rd Semester. The subject focuses on the planning, coordination, movement, and control of materials, information, inventory, and finished goods across suppliers, manufacturers, warehouses, distributors, retailers, and customers.

Practicing AKTU MBA 3rd Sem Supply Chain And Logistics Management PYQs helps students understand how supply-chain concepts, logistics systems, inventory decisions, transportation, warehousing, sourcing, distribution, and performance-management topics are framed in university examinations. Since the subject combines operations theory with practical managerial applications, students should prepare both concepts and real business examples carefully.

Students can explore AKTU MBA previous-year question papers and related academic resources on NotesGallery. For official university notices, examination announcements, academic circulars, and authoritative information, students should refer to the AKTU Official Website.

AKTU MBA 3rd Semester Subject Details

The subject details are:

Subject Code Subject Name Specialization
BMB OM 01 Supply Chain And Logistics Management Operation Management

Supply Chain And Logistics Management is part of the Operation Management specialization in MBA Semester 3.

The other Operation Management specialization subjects shown alongside it are:

Code Subject
BMB OM 02 Business Process Reengineering
BMB OM 03 Quality Management

MBA 3rd Semester also includes the core subject Strategic Management (BMB301) along with specialization electives from Marketing, Human Resource Management, Financial Management, International Business, Information Technology, and Cooperative Management.

About Supply Chain Management

Supply Chain Management refers to the coordination of all activities involved in the flow of materials, information, finances, and products from suppliers to final customers.

A typical supply chain may include:

Supplier → Manufacturer → Warehouse → Distributor → Retailer → Customer

The objective is to deliver the right product:

  • in the right quantity
  • at the right place
  • at the right time
  • at the right cost
  • with the expected quality

Supply Chain Management therefore involves much more than transportation.

Importance of Supply Chain Management

Effective supply-chain management can help organisations:

  • reduce operating cost
  • improve customer service
  • reduce inventory
  • improve delivery speed
  • strengthen supplier relationships
  • improve coordination
  • reduce waste
  • respond quickly to demand changes

In competitive markets, supply-chain efficiency can become an important source of business advantage.

Objectives of Supply Chain Management

Major objectives may include:

  • ensuring product availability
  • reducing total supply-chain cost
  • improving responsiveness
  • maintaining quality
  • minimising delays
  • improving coordination
  • reducing uncertainty
  • increasing customer satisfaction

The goal is to optimise the overall system rather than only one activity.

Supply Chain Members

Important participants in a supply chain may include:

  • suppliers
  • manufacturers
  • warehouses
  • distributors
  • wholesalers
  • retailers
  • logistics providers
  • customers

Each participant contributes to the movement and availability of products.

Supply Chain Flows

Supply chains involve several types of flows.

Product Flow

Product flow includes movement of:

  • raw materials
  • work-in-process
  • finished goods
  • returned products

Information Flow

Information may include:

  • customer orders
  • demand forecasts
  • inventory information
  • delivery status
  • production schedules

Financial Flow

Financial flow may include:

  • payments
  • credit terms
  • invoices
  • financial settlements

Effective supply chains require coordination of all three flows.

Meaning of Logistics

Logistics refers to planning, implementing, and controlling the movement and storage of goods and related information.

It may include:

  • transportation
  • warehousing
  • inventory
  • order processing
  • packaging
  • material handling
  • distribution

Logistics is an important part of the broader supply chain.

Supply Chain Management vs Logistics

Supply Chain Management Logistics
Broader concept A component of supply-chain management
Coordinates multiple organisations and activities Focuses mainly on movement and storage
Includes suppliers, manufacturing, distribution, and customers Includes transportation, warehousing, inventory, and delivery
Strategic and integrated More focused on operational flow

Students should clearly understand this distinction.

Inbound Logistics

Inbound logistics deals with movement of materials from suppliers into the organisation.

It may include:

  • procurement
  • transportation
  • receiving
  • storage of raw materials

Efficient inbound logistics helps reduce production delays.

Outbound Logistics

Outbound logistics deals with movement of finished goods from the organisation to customers.

It may include:

  • warehousing
  • order processing
  • transportation
  • distribution
  • delivery

The quality of outbound logistics directly affects customer satisfaction.

Procurement

Procurement involves acquiring goods and services required by an organisation.

It may include:

  • identifying requirements
  • selecting suppliers
  • negotiating terms
  • placing orders
  • monitoring delivery
  • evaluating suppliers

Procurement decisions influence cost, quality, and supply reliability.

Purchasing vs Procurement

Purchasing Procurement
Focuses mainly on buying Broader strategic process
Includes ordering and payment Includes sourcing, negotiation, supplier selection, and relationship management
More transactional More strategic

Supplier Selection

Supplier selection is an important supply-chain decision.

Suppliers may be evaluated based on:

  • price
  • quality
  • delivery reliability
  • capacity
  • location
  • technology
  • financial stability
  • service

The lowest-price supplier is not always the best choice if quality or reliability is poor.

Supplier Relationship Management

Supplier Relationship Management focuses on developing effective relationships with suppliers.

Strong supplier relationships can support:

  • better quality
  • timely delivery
  • joint problem-solving
  • innovation
  • lower risk

Long-term relationships may create more value than purely transactional purchasing.

Strategic Sourcing

Strategic sourcing is a systematic approach to selecting and managing suppliers in alignment with organisational strategy.

It may involve:

  • analysing spending
  • evaluating supply markets
  • selecting suppliers
  • negotiating contracts
  • monitoring performance

The aim is to improve value rather than simply reduce purchase price.

Make-or-Buy Decision

A make-or-buy decision determines whether a company should:

  • produce an item internally

or

  • purchase it from an external supplier

Factors may include:

  • cost
  • quality
  • capacity
  • expertise
  • confidentiality
  • supplier reliability
  • strategic importance

Outsourcing

Outsourcing means assigning certain activities to external organisations.

Companies may outsource:

  • transportation
  • warehousing
  • manufacturing
  • customer support
  • IT services

Potential benefits include cost reduction and access to specialised expertise.

However, outsourcing may also reduce control and increase dependency.

Third-Party Logistics

A Third-Party Logistics provider (3PL) performs logistics activities for another organisation.

Services may include:

  • transportation
  • warehousing
  • distribution
  • fulfilment

3PL providers allow companies to use external logistics expertise and infrastructure.

Demand Forecasting

Demand forecasting estimates future customer demand.

It helps in:

  • production planning
  • inventory planning
  • procurement
  • transportation
  • workforce planning

Poor forecasts can result in:

  • excess stock
  • shortages
  • higher cost
  • delayed deliveries

Demand Management

Demand management involves understanding and influencing customer demand.

It may include:

  • forecasting
  • promotions
  • pricing
  • order management
  • coordination with sales

Demand information should be shared throughout the supply chain.

Bullwhip Effect

The Bullwhip Effect occurs when small changes in customer demand create increasingly larger fluctuations in orders as information moves upstream in the supply chain.

It may lead to:

  • excess inventory
  • shortages
  • production instability
  • higher cost

Common causes may include:

  • inaccurate forecasting
  • order batching
  • price fluctuations
  • poor information sharing

Reducing the Bullwhip Effect

The Bullwhip Effect can be reduced through:

  • better information sharing
  • improved forecasting
  • smaller order batches
  • stable pricing
  • closer supplier coordination

Inventory Management

Inventory Management deals with controlling stock levels to balance product availability and cost.

Inventory may include:

  • raw materials
  • work-in-process
  • finished goods
  • spare parts

Too much inventory increases cost, while too little inventory may cause shortages.

Objectives of Inventory Management

Important objectives include:

  • avoid stockouts
  • minimise holding cost
  • maintain production continuity
  • support customer service
  • reduce excess stock

Inventory Costs

Inventory-related costs may include:

  • ordering cost
  • carrying cost
  • storage cost
  • shortage cost
  • obsolescence cost

Inventory decisions should consider the total cost rather than one cost alone.

Economic Order Quantity

Economic Order Quantity (EOQ) is a concept used to determine an order quantity that balances ordering and carrying costs.

Students should understand:

  • objective of EOQ
  • basic assumptions
  • relationship between ordering cost and holding cost
  • managerial importance

Where numerical questions are included, students should practice calculations carefully.

Reorder Level

The reorder level indicates when a new inventory order should be placed.

It is influenced by:

  • usage
  • lead time
  • safety stock

The purpose is to reduce the risk of stockouts.

Safety Stock

Safety stock is extra inventory maintained to protect against uncertainty.

It may be useful when:

  • demand fluctuates
  • supplier delivery is uncertain
  • lead time varies

Safety stock improves service levels but also increases inventory cost.

Just-in-Time

Just-in-Time (JIT) aims to reduce inventory by receiving or producing items close to the time they are needed.

Potential benefits include:

  • lower inventory
  • reduced storage
  • less waste
  • improved process efficiency

However, JIT requires reliable suppliers and efficient coordination.

Warehousing

Warehousing refers to storing goods until they are needed.

Warehouses may support:

  • storage
  • consolidation
  • order fulfilment
  • distribution
  • customer service

Warehouse decisions influence both cost and delivery speed.

Functions of Warehousing

Important functions include:

  • receiving
  • storage
  • picking
  • packing
  • dispatch
  • inventory control

Modern warehouses may also provide value-added services.

Warehouse Location

Warehouse location decisions may consider:

  • customer location
  • transportation cost
  • supplier location
  • land cost
  • service level
  • infrastructure

A poorly located warehouse can increase transportation cost and delivery time.

Warehouse Layout

An efficient warehouse layout helps:

  • reduce material movement
  • improve space utilisation
  • speed up picking
  • improve safety

Layout decisions should support the flow of goods.

Material Handling

Material handling involves moving goods within facilities.

It may include:

  • loading
  • unloading
  • movement
  • storage
  • picking

Efficient material handling reduces damage, time, and labour cost.

Transportation

Transportation is a major logistics activity.

It moves products between:

  • suppliers
  • factories
  • warehouses
  • distributors
  • customers

Transportation decisions influence:

  • cost
  • speed
  • reliability
  • customer service

Modes of Transportation

Common transportation modes include:

  • road
  • rail
  • air
  • water
  • pipeline

The appropriate mode depends on:

  • product
  • distance
  • cost
  • urgency
  • volume
  • reliability requirements

Road Transportation

Road transport is often flexible and suitable for door-to-door delivery.

Advantages may include:

  • flexibility
  • accessibility
  • suitable for shorter distances

Rail Transportation

Rail can be suitable for:

  • bulk goods
  • long-distance transportation
  • large quantities

It may provide lower cost for certain shipments.

Air Transportation

Air transport is generally fast but expensive.

It may be suitable for:

  • urgent shipments
  • high-value products
  • time-sensitive goods

Water Transportation

Water transport is often suitable for large quantities and international trade.

It can be economical but relatively slower.

Transportation Decision

Managers may select transport based on:

  • cost
  • speed
  • reliability
  • capacity
  • product characteristics
  • customer expectations

The cheapest mode may not always provide the lowest total supply-chain cost.

Distribution Management

Distribution Management ensures that products reach customers through suitable channels.

It may involve:

  • warehouses
  • distributors
  • wholesalers
  • retailers
  • transportation

Distribution strategy should support customer availability and cost efficiency.

Distribution Network

A distribution network describes how products move from production facilities to customers.

Possible structures may involve:

  • direct delivery
  • warehouses
  • distribution centres
  • retailers
  • e-commerce fulfilment centres

The network should balance cost and service.

Distribution Centre

A distribution centre focuses on receiving, processing, and quickly distributing goods.

It may provide:

  • consolidation
  • sorting
  • order fulfilment
  • cross-docking
  • dispatch

Cross-Docking

Cross-Docking is a logistics practice in which goods are transferred from incoming transportation to outgoing transportation with limited storage.

Potential benefits include:

  • reduced inventory
  • lower storage cost
  • faster movement

It requires strong coordination.

Order Processing

Order processing includes activities from receiving an order to final delivery.

It may involve:

  1. Order receipt
  2. Verification
  3. Inventory checking
  4. Picking and packing
  5. Dispatch
  6. Delivery
  7. Confirmation

Fast and accurate order processing improves customer satisfaction.

Order Fulfilment

Order fulfilment is the complete process of completing a customer order.

It may include:

  • inventory allocation
  • picking
  • packing
  • shipping
  • delivery

Order fulfilment is especially important in e-commerce.

Lead Time

Lead Time is the time between initiating an activity and completing it.

Examples include:

  • supplier lead time
  • production lead time
  • delivery lead time

Lower and more predictable lead time improves supply-chain responsiveness.

Customer Service in Logistics

Logistics customer service may involve:

  • product availability
  • delivery speed
  • delivery accuracy
  • order visibility
  • return handling

Customer service should be considered when evaluating logistics performance.

Reverse Logistics

Reverse Logistics deals with movement of goods from customers back toward the organisation or supply chain.

It may involve:

  • returns
  • repairs
  • recycling
  • reuse
  • disposal

Reverse logistics has become increasingly important in e-commerce and sustainability.

Supply Chain Integration

Supply-chain integration means coordinating activities across different supply-chain partners.

Integration may improve:

  • information sharing
  • planning
  • inventory
  • delivery
  • responsiveness

Poor integration can create delays and excess cost.

Internal Integration

Internal integration involves coordination among departments such as:

  • purchasing
  • production
  • marketing
  • finance
  • logistics

Departments should not make supply-chain decisions independently without considering broader effects.

External Integration

External integration involves coordination with:

  • suppliers
  • logistics providers
  • distributors
  • customers

It supports better planning and visibility.

Information Technology in Supply Chains

Technology helps manage complex supply chains.

Applications may include:

  • Enterprise Resource Planning
  • Warehouse Management Systems
  • Transportation Management Systems
  • tracking systems
  • electronic data exchange
  • analytics

Technology improves visibility and coordination.

Enterprise Resource Planning

Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) systems integrate information across business functions.

They may connect:

  • purchasing
  • inventory
  • production
  • sales
  • finance

Integrated data supports better supply-chain decisions.

Warehouse Management System

A Warehouse Management System (WMS) helps manage warehouse operations such as:

  • receiving
  • inventory location
  • picking
  • packing
  • dispatch

It can improve warehouse accuracy and efficiency.

Transportation Management System

A Transportation Management System (TMS) may support:

  • route planning
  • carrier selection
  • shipment tracking
  • transportation cost analysis

Supply Chain Visibility

Supply-chain visibility refers to the ability to track products, inventory, orders, and activities across the supply chain.

Better visibility helps managers identify:

  • delays
  • shortages
  • disruptions
  • bottlenecks

Supply Chain Analytics

Supply-chain analytics uses data to support decisions involving:

  • demand
  • inventory
  • transportation
  • supplier performance
  • delivery

Analytics can help improve forecasting and operational efficiency.

Supply Chain Risk

Supply chains face risks such as:

  • supplier failure
  • transportation disruption
  • natural disasters
  • demand uncertainty
  • political events
  • cyber incidents

Risk management has become an important part of supply-chain strategy.

Supply Chain Risk Management

A basic risk-management process may include:

  1. Identify risk
  2. Assess probability and impact
  3. Develop mitigation measures
  4. Monitor risk
  5. Respond to disruption

Possible mitigation measures may include:

  • multiple suppliers
  • safety stock
  • alternative transportation
  • contingency planning

Supply Chain Resilience

Supply-chain resilience is the ability to prepare for, respond to, and recover from disruptions.

A resilient supply chain may use:

  • supplier diversification
  • flexible capacity
  • alternative routes
  • visibility
  • contingency plans

Sustainable Supply Chain

A sustainable supply chain considers economic, environmental, and social factors.

Possible practices include:

  • reducing waste
  • improving energy efficiency
  • responsible sourcing
  • reducing emissions
  • recycling

Sustainability should be considered alongside cost and service.

Green Logistics

Green Logistics focuses on reducing environmental impact from logistics activities.

It may involve:

  • fuel efficiency
  • route optimisation
  • sustainable packaging
  • recycling
  • lower-emission transportation

Global Supply Chain

A global supply chain involves sourcing, production, or distribution across multiple countries.

It may create benefits such as:

  • lower cost
  • access to global suppliers
  • market expansion

However, it may also increase:

  • lead time
  • complexity
  • political risk
  • currency exposure
  • disruption risk

E-Commerce Logistics

E-commerce has changed traditional logistics requirements.

Important considerations include:

  • fast delivery
  • fulfilment centres
  • last-mile delivery
  • order tracking
  • returns

Customers increasingly expect greater delivery speed and visibility.

Last-Mile Delivery

Last-mile delivery refers to the final movement of a product from a distribution facility to the customer.

It is often one of the most expensive and challenging parts of e-commerce logistics.

Challenges may include:

  • traffic
  • failed deliveries
  • dispersed customers
  • delivery expectations

Supply Chain Performance Measurement

Supply-chain performance can be evaluated through metrics such as:

  • order fulfilment time
  • inventory turnover
  • delivery accuracy
  • logistics cost
  • stockout rate
  • supplier performance
  • customer service level

Managers should use multiple measures rather than relying on one metric.

Inventory Turnover

Inventory turnover indicates how frequently inventory is sold or used during a period.

A higher turnover may indicate efficient inventory use, but interpretation depends on the business.

Very high turnover may also indicate insufficient stock.

Service Level

Service level reflects the organisation’s ability to meet customer demand.

It may be evaluated through:

  • product availability
  • order fulfilment
  • delivery reliability

Higher service often requires additional cost, so managers must balance service and efficiency.

Total Logistics Cost

Managers should evaluate total logistics cost rather than reducing one cost in isolation.

For example:

  • reducing warehouse inventory may increase transport frequency
  • cheaper transport may increase delivery time
  • additional warehouses may improve service but increase fixed cost

The objective is overall optimisation.

Relationship With Business Process Reengineering

Supply Chain And Logistics Management connects directly with Business Process Reengineering (BMB OM 02).

Reengineering may be used to redesign supply-chain processes such as:

  • procurement
  • order fulfilment
  • warehouse operations
  • distribution

The goal may be major improvement in cost, speed, quality, or service.

Relationship With Quality Management

It also connects with Quality Management (BMB OM 03).

Supply chains depend on:

  • supplier quality
  • process quality
  • delivery accuracy
  • product condition

Poor quality at any stage can affect the final customer.

Relationship With Strategic Management

The core subject Strategic Management (BMB301) connects strongly with supply-chain decisions.

Supply-chain capabilities can support strategies based on:

  • low cost
  • differentiation
  • speed
  • responsiveness
  • customer service

Supply Chain Management can therefore contribute directly to competitive advantage.

Improve Application-Based Thinking

  • transportation

  • order processing

How to Practice Supply Chain And Logistics Management PYQs

Step 1: Understand the Concept

Study the topic and understand its role in the overall supply chain.

Step 2: Learn the Process

For process-oriented topics, understand the logical sequence.

Step 3: Attempt Related PYQs

Write the answer independently without referring to notes.

Step 4: Structure the Answer

A useful format is:

  1. Definition
  2. Objectives
  3. Process or components
  4. Advantages
  5. Limitations
  6. Managerial application

Step 5: Use Diagrams Where Appropriate

Simple flow diagrams can improve answers for topics such as:

  • supply chain
  • logistics flow
  • distribution network
  • order fulfilment

Step 6: Prepare Comparison Tables

Prepare short tables for concepts that are easy to confuse.

Step 7: Solve a Complete Paper

After syllabus revision, attempt a full previous-year paper within a fixed time.

This improves:

  • recall
  • answer structure
  • managerial understanding
  • application of concepts
  • time management

Quick Revision Strategy

For final revision, divide the subject into four broad areas.

Supply Chain Fundamentals

Revise:

  • meaning
  • objectives
  • members
  • flows
  • integration

Inventory and Warehousing

Revise:

  • inventory
  • EOQ
  • reorder level
  • safety stock
  • JIT
  • warehousing
  • material handling

Logistics and Distribution

Revise:

  • inbound logistics
  • outbound logistics
  • transportation
  • distribution
  • order processing
  • 3PL
  • reverse logistics

Modern Supply Chain Management

Revise:

  • Bullwhip Effect
  • analytics
  • ERP
  • WMS
  • risk
  • resilience
  • sustainability
  • e-commerce
  • last-mile delivery

After revision, attempt selected PYQs without referring to your notes.

Business Process Reengineering is an important Operation Management specialization subject in AKTU MBA 3rd Semester. The subject focuses on the fundamental redesign of business processes to achieve major improvements in performance, cost, quality, speed, productivity, and customer service.

Students can explore AKTU MBA previous-year question papers and related academic resources on NotesGallery. For official university notices, examination announcements, academic circulars, and authoritative information, students should refer to the AKTU Official Website.

AKTU MBA 3rd Semester Subject Details

The subject details are:

Subject Code Subject Name Specialization
BMB OM 02 Business Process Reengineering Operation Management

Business Process Reengineering is part of the Operation Management specialization in MBA Semester 3.

The other Operation Management specialization subjects shown alongside it are:

Code Subject
BMB OM 01 Supply Chain and Logistics Management
BMB OM 03 Quality Management

MBA 3rd Semester also includes the core subject Strategic Management (BMB301) along with specialization electives from Marketing, Human Resource Management, Financial Management, International Business, Information Technology, and Cooperative Management.

About Business Process Reengineering

Business Process Reengineering, commonly referred to as BPR, focuses on analysing and fundamentally redesigning business processes to achieve significant performance improvements.

A business process is a sequence of activities that converts inputs into outputs for customers or other stakeholders.

Examples may include:

  • order processing
  • procurement
  • customer service
  • production
  • billing
  • recruitment
  • inventory handling

BPR examines whether such processes can be redesigned rather than simply improved slightly.

Meaning of Business Process

A business process is a set of related activities performed to achieve a specific organisational objective.

A simple process may be represented as:

Input → Activities → Output

For example:

Customer Order → Verification → Processing → Packing → Delivery

The effectiveness of the complete process matters more than isolated departmental performance.

Meaning of Reengineering

Reengineering means critically examining an existing process and redesigning it in a major way.

It may involve:

  • eliminating unnecessary activities
  • combining tasks
  • reducing approvals
  • using technology
  • changing responsibilities
  • simplifying workflows

The aim is to achieve substantial rather than minor improvement.

Meaning of Business Process Reengineering

Business Process Reengineering can be understood as the fundamental reconsideration and redesign of business processes to achieve major improvements in important performance measures.

These measures may include:

  • cost
  • quality
  • service
  • speed
  • productivity

BPR asks organisations to reconsider how work should be performed rather than simply improving the existing method.

Objectives of BPR

Important objectives of Business Process Reengineering may include:

  • reducing process time
  • reducing cost
  • eliminating duplication
  • improving customer service
  • improving quality
  • increasing productivity
  • simplifying operations
  • improving flexibility

The exact objective depends on the business problem being addressed.

Need for Business Process Reengineering

Organisations may consider BPR when:

  • processes are too slow
  • costs are excessive
  • customers are dissatisfied
  • technology has changed
  • competition has increased
  • work is highly fragmented
  • excessive approvals create delay

BPR is particularly relevant when incremental improvement may not be sufficient.

Characteristics of BPR

Important characteristics may include:

  • process orientation
  • radical redesign
  • major improvement
  • customer focus
  • use of technology
  • cross-functional thinking
  • simplification

BPR looks at the organisation through complete processes rather than isolated functions.

Fundamental Rethinking

BPR begins by questioning existing assumptions.

Managers may ask:

  • Why is this activity performed?
  • Does the customer value it?
  • Can it be eliminated?
  • Can multiple steps be combined?
  • Can technology automate it?

This approach helps organisations challenge outdated practices.

Radical Redesign

Radical redesign means making major changes rather than minor adjustments.

It may involve:

  • eliminating entire steps
  • redesigning workflows
  • changing roles
  • restructuring responsibilities
  • introducing technology

The objective is to create a significantly better process.

Dramatic Improvement

BPR aims for substantial improvement in areas such as:

  • cost
  • cycle time
  • service
  • quality

This is one major difference between BPR and gradual process improvement.

Process Orientation

Traditional organisations may focus on departments such as:

  • finance
  • marketing
  • operations
  • HR

BPR focuses on end-to-end processes that may cross several departments.

For example, fulfilling a customer order may involve:

  • sales
  • finance
  • inventory
  • logistics

The complete process should be evaluated as one system.

Customer Focus

BPR often begins with the customer.

Managers may ask:

  • What does the customer value?
  • Which steps improve customer experience?
  • Which steps create delay without adding value?

Customer-focused redesign can improve both service and competitiveness.

Principles of Business Process Reengineering

Common principles associated with BPR may include:

  • organise around outcomes
  • reduce unnecessary handoffs
  • combine related activities
  • capture information once
  • use technology effectively
  • move decision-making closer to the work
  • focus on customer value

Students should understand the logic behind these principles.

BPR Process

A general Business Process Reengineering process may include:

  1. Identify processes
  2. Select processes for redesign
  3. Understand existing process
  4. Identify problems and non-value-added activities
  5. Design a new process
  6. Use suitable technology
  7. Implement the redesigned process
  8. Measure results

The exact sequence may differ among organisations.

Process Identification

The first step is to identify important organisational processes.

Examples include:

  • order fulfilment
  • procurement
  • product development
  • recruitment
  • complaint handling

Managers should identify which processes contribute most directly to performance and customer value.

Process Selection

Not every process requires radical redesign.

Processes may be selected based on:

  • high cost
  • long delays
  • poor quality
  • customer complaints
  • strategic importance
  • competitive pressure

Priority should be given to processes with significant improvement potential.

Existing Process Analysis

Before redesigning a process, managers should understand how it currently works.

This may involve:

  • mapping activities
  • identifying delays
  • measuring time
  • examining approvals
  • locating bottlenecks

Understanding the current state helps reveal unnecessary complexity.

Process Mapping

Process Mapping visually represents the steps involved in a business process.

A simple map may show:

Start → Activity 1 → Decision → Activity 2 → Output

Process maps help identify:

  • duplication
  • delays
  • unnecessary approvals
  • bottlenecks
  • rework

They make complex workflows easier to understand.

Value-Added Activities

A value-added activity contributes directly to an outcome valued by the customer or organisation.

Examples may include:

  • creating the product
  • processing necessary information
  • delivering customer service

BPR seeks to maximise useful activities and minimise waste.

Non-Value-Added Activities

Non-value-added activities consume time or resources without creating sufficient value.

Examples may include:

  • unnecessary approvals
  • duplicate data entry
  • excessive waiting
  • repeated verification

Removing these activities can improve process performance.

Bottlenecks

A bottleneck is a point in a process where work slows down because capacity or efficiency is limited.

Bottlenecks may result in:

  • delays
  • queues
  • higher cost
  • poor customer service

Identifying bottlenecks is important in process redesign.

Process Redesign

Process redesign involves creating a better workflow.

Possible actions may include:

  • removing steps
  • combining tasks
  • automating activities
  • reducing handoffs
  • decentralising decisions
  • redesigning roles

The redesigned process should support customer and organisational objectives.

Role of Information Technology in BPR

Information Technology is one of the most important enablers of BPR.

Technology can help organisations:

  • automate routine work
  • integrate departments
  • share information instantly
  • reduce paperwork
  • improve customer access
  • support faster decisions

Technology should support redesigned processes rather than simply automate inefficient old processes.

Information Systems and Process Integration

Integrated information systems can connect activities across departments.

For example, an order-processing system may connect:

  • sales
  • inventory
  • finance
  • logistics

This can reduce duplicate data entry and improve information flow.

Enterprise Resource Planning

Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) systems integrate business functions through a common information platform.

ERP may connect:

  • purchasing
  • production
  • inventory
  • finance
  • HR
  • sales

ERP can support BPR by enabling integrated processes.

Automation

Automation uses technology to perform repetitive or rule-based activities.

It may help reduce:

  • manual effort
  • errors
  • processing time
  • operating cost

Automation is most effective after the process itself has been reviewed and simplified.

Digital Transformation and BPR

Digital transformation can create opportunities for radical process redesign.

Technologies may enable:

  • digital workflows
  • online services
  • real-time data
  • automated approvals
  • analytics
  • remote collaboration

BPR can therefore support broader organisational transformation.

BPR and Organisational Structure

Process redesign may require changes in organisational structure.

Traditional structures may contain:

  • many hierarchical levels
  • specialised departments
  • multiple approvals

BPR may support:

  • flatter structures
  • cross-functional teams
  • greater employee responsibility
  • faster decision-making

Cross-Functional Teams

A cross-functional team includes employees from different functional areas.

Such teams can be useful in BPR because processes often cross departmental boundaries.

For example, order fulfilment may involve representatives from:

  • sales
  • finance
  • operations
  • logistics

This improves coordination.

Employee Empowerment

BPR may give employees greater decision-making authority.

Empowerment can:

  • reduce approval delays
  • improve responsiveness
  • increase responsibility
  • support customer service

Employees need suitable training and information to handle greater responsibility effectively.

Role of Top Management in BPR

Top management support is critical because BPR may require:

  • major investment
  • structural change
  • technology
  • employee involvement
  • strategic decisions

Leadership must communicate why change is necessary.

Role of Employees in BPR

Employees often understand practical process problems better than senior managers.

Their involvement can help:

  • identify inefficiencies
  • improve process design
  • reduce resistance
  • increase acceptance

Ignoring employees can weaken implementation.

Change Management in BPR

BPR involves significant change.

Employees may resist because of:

  • fear of job loss
  • uncertainty
  • changed responsibilities
  • unfamiliar technology
  • lack of communication

Change management is therefore an important part of BPR.

Resistance to Change

Resistance can be reduced through:

  • communication
  • employee involvement
  • training
  • leadership support
  • clear explanation of benefits
  • gradual preparation

Managers should address both technical and human aspects of redesign.

Organisational Culture and BPR

Organisational culture influences how employees respond to process changes.

A culture that supports:

  • innovation
  • collaboration
  • learning
  • customer focus

can make BPR implementation easier.

A highly rigid culture may create resistance.

Benchmarking

Benchmarking involves comparing organisational processes or performance with leading practices or standards.

It can help identify:

  • performance gaps
  • improvement opportunities
  • better methods

Benchmarking may provide ideas for process redesign.

Types of Benchmarking

Broad forms may include:

  • internal benchmarking
  • competitive benchmarking
  • functional benchmarking
  • generic benchmarking

Students should understand the purpose of each where covered in their syllabus.

Internal Benchmarking

Internal benchmarking compares similar activities within the same organisation.

It can help identify which unit performs more effectively.

Competitive Benchmarking

Competitive benchmarking compares performance or practices with competitors.

It helps organisations understand their relative position.

Functional Benchmarking

Functional benchmarking compares a business function with organisations recognised for strong performance in that area.

The organisations being compared may operate in different industries.

BPR vs Continuous Improvement

Business Process Reengineering and continuous improvement are different approaches.

BPR Continuous Improvement
Radical change Incremental change
Major redesign Small repeated improvements
Often high impact Gradual improvement
May change complete processes Improves existing processes
Usually less frequent Ongoing

Both approaches can be useful depending on the situation.

BPR vs Total Quality Management

BPR and Total Quality Management both aim to improve organisational performance but differ in approach.

BPR Total Quality Management
Focuses on radical redesign Focuses on continuous quality improvement
Often redesigns entire processes Improves existing processes systematically
May involve major structural change Emphasises ongoing participation
Seeks dramatic improvement Seeks consistent long-term improvement

They can complement each other.

BPR vs Business Process Improvement

Business Process Improvement usually focuses on gradually improving existing processes.

BPR focuses on more fundamental redesign.

The choice depends on:

  • severity of problems
  • strategic objectives
  • available resources
  • urgency

BPR and Quality

Process redesign can improve quality by:

  • reducing errors
  • eliminating duplication
  • simplifying work
  • increasing accountability
  • improving information accuracy

Poor processes often create quality problems even when employees work hard.

BPR and Cost Reduction

BPR can reduce costs by:

  • eliminating unnecessary activities
  • reducing paperwork
  • automating routine work
  • shortening cycle time
  • improving resource utilisation

However, cost reduction should not damage customer value.

BPR and Cycle Time

Cycle Time is the total time required to complete a process.

Examples may include:

  • order-to-delivery time
  • recruitment time
  • complaint-resolution time

Reducing cycle time is a common BPR objective.

BPR and Customer Service

Process redesign can improve customer service by:

  • reducing waiting
  • simplifying procedures
  • improving information
  • speeding delivery
  • reducing errors

Customer experience should be considered when redesigning processes.

Performance Measures in BPR

After implementation, managers should measure whether the redesigned process has improved.

Possible measures include:

  • processing time
  • cost
  • error rate
  • customer satisfaction
  • productivity
  • service level

The measures should match the objectives of the redesign.

Key Performance Indicators in BPR

KPIs may be used to monitor redesigned processes.

Examples may include:

  • order fulfilment time
  • cost per transaction
  • customer complaints
  • error percentage
  • productivity

Comparing results before and after redesign helps evaluate success.

Business Process Management

Business Process Management (BPM) focuses on continuously managing and improving organisational processes.

BPR and BPM are related, but BPR usually involves more radical redesign.

BPM may involve:

  • process modelling
  • monitoring
  • optimisation
  • continuous control

BPR vs BPM

BPR BPM
Often radical Usually continuous
Used for major redesign Used for ongoing process management
May be project-based More continuous in nature
Focuses on transformation Focuses on monitoring and optimisation

BPR Success Factors

Factors supporting successful BPR may include:

  • top management support
  • clear objectives
  • strong leadership
  • employee involvement
  • suitable technology
  • adequate resources
  • effective communication
  • performance measurement

Reasons for BPR Failure

BPR initiatives may fail because of:

  • unclear objectives
  • lack of management support
  • employee resistance
  • poor communication
  • insufficient resources
  • excessive focus on technology
  • weak implementation
  • unrealistic expectations

Understanding failure factors is important because BPR projects can involve significant organisational risk.

BPR Implementation

A successful implementation requires coordination among:

  • management
  • employees
  • technology teams
  • process owners

Implementation may involve:

  1. Communicating redesigned process
  2. Training employees
  3. Installing required technology
  4. Testing the new process
  5. Monitoring results
  6. Correcting problems

Process Owner

A Process Owner is a person responsible for the performance of an end-to-end business process.

The process owner may:

  • monitor results
  • coordinate departments
  • identify improvements
  • ensure accountability

This role supports process-oriented management.

Business Process Reengineering in Manufacturing

Manufacturing organisations may use BPR to redesign:

  • procurement
  • production
  • inventory
  • quality control
  • distribution

The objective may be to reduce lead time and improve productivity.

BPR in Service Organisations

Service organisations may redesign processes such as:

  • customer onboarding
  • billing
  • complaint handling
  • approvals
  • service delivery

Service BPR often focuses strongly on customer experience and response time.

BPR in Banking

Banks may apply BPR to:

  • account opening
  • loan processing
  • customer service
  • transaction processing

Digital banking has enabled many traditionally manual processes to be redesigned.

BPR in Healthcare

Healthcare organisations may redesign:

  • patient registration
  • appointment scheduling
  • billing
  • record management

The objective can include faster service and improved coordination.

BPR in Human Resource Management

HR processes that may be redesigned include:

  • recruitment
  • onboarding
  • leave approval
  • payroll
  • performance management

Technology can significantly reduce manual HR administration.

BPR in Supply Chain Management

Business Process Reengineering connects directly with Supply Chain and Logistics Management (BMB OM 01).

Supply-chain processes such as:

  • purchasing
  • inventory management
  • order fulfilment
  • transportation
  • warehouse operations

can be redesigned to reduce cost and improve speed.

Relationship With Quality Management

BPR also connects closely with Quality Management (BMB OM 03).

Quality Management focuses strongly on consistency and improvement, while BPR may redesign the complete process when incremental improvement is not sufficient.

Both approaches can support:

  • customer satisfaction
  • lower errors
  • higher productivity

Relationship With Strategic Management

The core subject Strategic Management (BMB301) connects strongly with BPR.

An organisation may redesign processes to support strategies based on:

  • cost leadership
  • customer service
  • speed
  • innovation
  • digital transformation

BPR should therefore align with overall organisational strategy.

Why Solve AKTU MBA Business Process Reengineering PYQs?

Understand the Examination Pattern

  • definitions

While practicing AKTU MBA 3rd Sem Business Process Reengineering PYQs, students should pay particular attention to:

  • meaning of business process
  • meaning of BPR
  • objectives of BPR
  • characteristics of BPR
  • principles of BPR
  • BPR process
  • process identification
  • process selection
  • process mapping
  • value-added activities
  • non-value-added activities
  • bottlenecks
  • process redesign
  • information technology in BPR
  • ERP
  • automation
  • digital transformation
  • organisational structure
  • cross-functional teams
  • employee empowerment
  • change management

  • organisational culture
  • benchmarking

  • BPR vs BPM

How to Practice Business Process Reengineering PYQs

Step 1: Understand the Process Perspective

Study how complete processes cross organisational departments.

Step 2: Learn the BPR Sequence

Understand:

Identify → Analyse → Redesign → Implement → Evaluate

Step 3: Attempt Related PYQs

Write answers without referring to notes.

Step 4: Use Process Diagrams

Simple diagrams can improve answers involving:

  • process flow
  • BPR stages
  • current vs redesigned process

Step 5: Prepare Comparison Tables

Comparison-based questions can be presented clearly using tables.

Step 6: Add Practical Applications

Where relevant, explain how BPR could improve a real organisational process.

Step 7: Solve a Complete Paper

After syllabus revision, attempt a complete previous-year paper within a fixed time.

This improves:

  • recall
  • conceptual clarity
  • answer structure
  • application of concepts
  • time management

BPR Fundamentals

  • employee empowerment

Implementation and Change

  • benchmarking

  • BPR vs BPM
  • success factors
  • reasons for failure

After revision, attempt selected PYQs without referring to your notes.

Business Process Reengineering is an MBA Operation Management specialization subject that focuses on fundamentally redesigning organisational processes to achieve major improvements in cost, quality, service, speed, and productivity.

Quality Management is an important Operation Management specialization subject in AKTU MBA 3rd Semester. The subject focuses on planning, controlling, assuring, and continuously improving quality in products, services, and business processes so that organisations can meet customer expectations and improve operational performance.

Practicing AKTU MBA 3rd Sem Quality Management PYQs helps students understand how quality concepts, quality-control tools, continuous improvement, Total Quality Management, statistical quality methods, quality standards, and process-improvement topics are framed in university examinations. Since the subject combines managerial concepts with analytical and process-oriented thinking, previous-year papers are useful for improving both conceptual clarity and answer-writing.

Students can explore AKTU MBA previous-year question papers and related academic resources on NotesGallery. For official university notices, examination announcements, academic circulars, and authoritative information, students should refer to the AKTU Official Website.

AKTU MBA 3rd Semester Subject Details

The subject details are:

Subject Code Subject Name Specialization
BMB OM 03 Quality Management Operation Management

Quality Management is part of the Operation Management specialization in MBA Semester 3.

The other Operation Management specialization subjects shown alongside it are:

Code Subject
BMB OM 01 Supply Chain and Logistics Management
BMB OM 02 Business Process Reengineering

MBA 3rd Semester also includes the core subject Strategic Management (BMB301) along with specialization electives from Marketing, Human Resource Management, Financial Management, International Business, Information Technology, and Cooperative Management.

About Quality Management

Quality Management refers to the systematic activities used by an organisation to ensure that products, services, and processes meet defined requirements and customer expectations.

It may include:

  • quality planning
  • quality control
  • quality assurance
  • quality improvement
  • quality measurement
  • customer feedback
  • process standardisation
  • defect prevention

The objective is not only to detect defects but also to prevent them and improve the overall system.

Meaning of Quality

Quality can be understood as the ability of a product or service to satisfy stated or implied customer requirements.

Quality may be associated with:

  • performance
  • reliability
  • durability
  • consistency
  • safety
  • service
  • customer satisfaction

Different customers may evaluate quality differently depending on their expectations.

Importance of Quality

Quality is important because it can help organisations:

  • improve customer satisfaction
  • reduce defects
  • reduce rework
  • lower cost
  • improve reputation
  • increase productivity
  • strengthen competitiveness
  • improve employee involvement

Poor quality can increase cost and damage long-term customer trust.

Dimensions of Quality

Quality may be evaluated through different dimensions depending on the product or service.

Common dimensions may include:

  • performance
  • features
  • reliability
  • conformance
  • durability
  • serviceability
  • aesthetics
  • perceived quality

Students should understand that quality is multi-dimensional rather than based on only one factor.

Quality Planning

Quality Planning involves deciding:

  • what quality standards are required
  • how quality will be achieved
  • what processes will be used
  • how performance will be measured

Quality planning should begin before production or service delivery.

Quality Control

Quality Control focuses on monitoring outputs and processes to identify whether quality standards are being met.

It may involve:

  • inspection
  • measurement
  • testing
  • process monitoring
  • corrective action

Quality control helps detect problems.

Quality Assurance

Quality Assurance focuses on designing systems and procedures that reduce the chance of quality problems occurring.

It may involve:

  • standard operating procedures
  • documentation
  • audits
  • process standards
  • training

Quality assurance is more preventive in nature.

Quality Control vs Quality Assurance

Quality Control Quality Assurance
Focuses on detecting defects Focuses on preventing defects
More output-oriented More process-oriented
Includes inspection and testing Includes systems and procedures
Reactive in many situations Preventive in nature

Quality Improvement

Quality improvement involves systematic efforts to improve existing processes, products, or services.

It may focus on:

  • reducing defects
  • reducing waste
  • improving speed
  • improving reliability
  • increasing customer satisfaction

Quality improvement should be continuous rather than occasional.

Total Quality Management

Total Quality Management (TQM) is an organisation-wide approach focused on continuous improvement, customer satisfaction, employee involvement, and process quality.

TQM emphasises that quality is the responsibility of everyone in the organisation.

Principles of Total Quality Management

Important principles may include:

  • customer focus
  • continuous improvement
  • employee involvement
  • process orientation
  • fact-based decision-making
  • leadership commitment
  • supplier relationships

Students should understand each principle rather than memorising only the list.

Customer Focus

Customer focus means understanding and meeting customer expectations.

Organisations may use:

  • surveys
  • complaints
  • feedback
  • market research

to understand customer requirements.

Quality should be evaluated from the customer’s point of view.

Continuous Improvement

Continuous improvement means making ongoing efforts to improve performance.

Small improvements over time can produce significant benefits.

The focus may include:

  • quality
  • cost
  • delivery
  • productivity
  • customer service

Kaizen

Kaizen refers to continuous and incremental improvement involving employees at different organisational levels.

Kaizen encourages:

  • small improvements
  • employee participation
  • waste reduction
  • process discipline

It is different from major one-time restructuring.

Employee Involvement

Employees often identify operational problems before senior managers.

Employee involvement can help:

  • generate improvement ideas
  • identify defects
  • improve processes
  • strengthen ownership

TQM therefore requires participation across the organisation.

Quality Culture

A quality culture exists when employees consistently value:

  • customer satisfaction
  • prevention
  • improvement
  • responsibility
  • teamwork

Quality culture depends strongly on leadership behaviour and organisational systems.

Role of Leadership in Quality

Management leadership is important because quality programmes require:

  • clear direction
  • resources
  • training
  • employee support
  • performance review

Without management commitment, quality initiatives may become temporary activities.

Deming and Quality Management

W. Edwards Deming is strongly associated with modern quality management and continuous improvement.

His work emphasised ideas such as:

  • process improvement
  • management responsibility
  • reduction of variation
  • long-term quality thinking

Students should understand his contribution conceptually.

Juran and Quality Management

Joseph Juran emphasised the managerial aspects of quality.

The Juran Trilogy is commonly associated with:

  • quality planning
  • quality control
  • quality improvement

This framework helps explain how quality should be managed systematically.

Crosby and Quality Management

Philip Crosby is associated with concepts such as:

  • prevention
  • conformance to requirements
  • zero defects

His approach emphasised reducing the cost created by poor quality.

Cost of Quality

The Cost of Quality includes costs related to achieving quality as well as costs caused by poor quality.

It can broadly include:

  • prevention cost
  • appraisal cost
  • internal failure cost
  • external failure cost

Prevention Cost

Prevention costs are incurred to stop defects from occurring.

Examples include:

  • training
  • process planning
  • quality-system design
  • supplier development

Appraisal Cost

Appraisal costs relate to measuring and evaluating quality.

Examples include:

  • inspection
  • testing
  • audits
  • quality checks

Internal Failure Cost

Internal failure costs occur when defects are discovered before the product reaches the customer.

Examples include:

  • scrap
  • rework
  • retesting
  • production delays

External Failure Cost

External failure costs occur after the product reaches the customer.

Examples include:

  • warranty claims
  • returns
  • complaints
  • loss of reputation

External failure can be particularly damaging because it affects customer trust.

Prevention vs Inspection

Modern quality approaches generally place strong emphasis on preventing defects rather than relying only on inspection.

Inspection detects problems after they occur, while prevention attempts to stop problems from being created.

Seven Basic Quality Tools

Quality management commonly uses several basic analytical tools.

These may include:

  • check sheet
  • histogram
  • Pareto chart
  • cause-and-effect diagram
  • scatter diagram
  • control chart
  • flowchart

These tools help managers understand process and quality problems.

Check Sheet

A Check Sheet is a structured form used to collect and organise data.

It may help identify:

  • frequency of defects
  • type of problems
  • location of problems

Check sheets make data collection systematic.

Histogram

A Histogram displays the frequency distribution of data.

It can help managers understand:

  • variation
  • concentration
  • spread
  • shape of data

Pareto Chart

A Pareto Chart helps identify the most significant causes or categories contributing to a problem.

It is associated with the idea that a relatively small number of causes may account for a large proportion of problems.

Managers can use it to prioritise improvement efforts.

Cause-and-Effect Diagram

The Cause-and-Effect Diagram, also called the Fishbone or Ishikawa Diagram, helps identify possible causes of a problem.

Possible categories may include:

  • people
  • machines
  • methods
  • materials
  • measurement
  • environment

It supports root-cause analysis.

Scatter Diagram

A scatter diagram shows the relationship between two variables.

It can help determine whether changes in one variable appear associated with changes in another.

Control Chart

A Control Chart helps monitor whether a process remains stable over time.

It usually includes:

  • centre line
  • upper control limit
  • lower control limit

Control charts help distinguish normal process variation from unusual variation.

Flowchart

A flowchart visually represents the sequence of steps in a process.

It helps identify:

  • delays
  • duplication
  • unnecessary activities
  • process complexity

Statistical Quality Control

Statistical Quality Control (SQC) uses statistical techniques to monitor and control quality.

It may include:

  • process control
  • acceptance sampling
  • control charts

The aim is to make quality decisions using data rather than only subjective judgement.

Statistical Process Control

Statistical Process Control (SPC) involves monitoring process behaviour using statistical methods.

The objective is to identify unusual variation before it causes large quality problems.

Process Variation

Variation exists in every process.

Variation may arise from:

  • machines
  • materials
  • people
  • methods
  • environment

Quality management attempts to understand and reduce unnecessary variation.

Common Cause Variation

Common cause variation is inherent in the existing process.

Reducing it often requires improvement to the overall system.

Special Cause Variation

Special cause variation results from specific unusual factors.

Examples may include:

  • machine breakdown
  • wrong material
  • operator error
  • unusual environmental condition

Identifying special causes is important for process control.

Common Cause vs Special Cause Variation

Common Cause Variation Special Cause Variation
Inherent in the process Caused by specific unusual factor
More predictable Less predictable
Requires system improvement Requires identification and correction of specific cause

Control Limits vs Specification Limits

Control limits and specification limits should not be confused.

Control limits are based on actual process behaviour.

Specification limits are based on customer, design, or engineering requirements.

A process may be statistically stable but still fail customer specifications.

Process Capability

Process capability refers to the ability of a stable process to produce output within required specifications.

A capable process consistently meets expected requirements.

Students should understand the concept and its connection with process variation.

Acceptance Sampling

Acceptance Sampling involves examining a sample from a batch or lot to decide whether the lot should be accepted or rejected.

It may be useful when:

  • 100% inspection is expensive
  • testing is destructive
  • large quantities are involved

Sampling involves risk, so it should be designed carefully.

Inspection

Inspection involves checking products, materials, or processes against standards.

Inspection may occur:

  • before production
  • during production
  • after production

Modern quality management aims to combine necessary inspection with stronger process control and prevention.

Quality Circles

A Quality Circle is a small group of employees who regularly meet to identify and solve work-related problems.

Quality circles can support:

  • employee participation
  • problem-solving
  • continuous improvement
  • teamwork

Benchmarking

Benchmarking involves comparing organisational performance or processes with recognised good practices.

It can help identify:

  • performance gaps
  • improvement opportunities
  • superior practices

Types of Benchmarking

Broad types may include:

  • internal benchmarking
  • competitive benchmarking
  • functional benchmarking
  • generic benchmarking

The objective is learning and improvement.

Six Sigma

Six Sigma is a data-driven approach focused on reducing defects and process variation.

It emphasises:

  • measurement
  • analysis
  • root-cause identification
  • process improvement

A commonly associated methodology is DMAIC.

DMAIC

DMAIC stands for:

  1. Define
  2. Measure
  3. Analyse
  4. Improve
  5. Control

Define

Identify the problem and customer requirements.

Measure

Collect data about current performance.

Analyse

Identify root causes of poor performance.

Improve

Develop and implement solutions.

Control

Maintain the improved process.

Six Sigma and Quality Improvement

Six Sigma can help organisations:

  • reduce defects
  • reduce variation
  • improve process capability
  • improve customer satisfaction

It relies strongly on data and measurement.

Lean Management

Lean Management focuses on creating customer value while reducing waste.

It attempts to remove activities that do not add value.

Waste may include:

  • waiting
  • unnecessary movement
  • excess inventory
  • defects
  • overproduction

Lean vs Six Sigma

Lean Six Sigma
Focuses strongly on waste reduction Focuses strongly on defect and variation reduction
Improves process flow Improves process consistency
Emphasises speed and efficiency Emphasises statistical analysis

The two approaches can also be combined.

Lean Six Sigma

Lean Six Sigma combines:

  • Lean’s focus on waste and flow
  • Six Sigma’s focus on variation and defects

The combined approach aims to improve:

  • quality
  • speed
  • cost
  • customer value

5S

5S is a workplace-organisation approach associated with Lean practices.

It focuses on:

  • organising the workplace
  • maintaining cleanliness
  • standardising practices
  • sustaining discipline

A well-organised workplace can support quality and productivity.

Poka-Yoke

Poka-Yoke refers to mistake-proofing.

The objective is to design processes so that:

  • errors are prevented

or

  • errors are detected immediately

Examples may include physical or digital controls that make incorrect action difficult.

Just-in-Time and Quality

Just-in-Time systems maintain relatively low inventory levels.

This increases the importance of:

  • supplier quality
  • process reliability
  • defect prevention

Poor quality can quickly disrupt a JIT system.

Quality Function Deployment

Quality Function Deployment (QFD) helps translate customer requirements into product or process characteristics.

Its purpose is to ensure that customer expectations influence design and development decisions.

Voice of Customer

The Voice of Customer represents customer:

  • needs
  • expectations
  • preferences
  • complaints
  • feedback

Quality programmes should incorporate customer information into improvement activities.

Customer Satisfaction

Customer satisfaction reflects the extent to which performance meets or exceeds expectations.

Satisfied customers may contribute to:

  • repeat purchases
  • loyalty
  • positive recommendations
  • stronger brand reputation

Quality and customer satisfaction are closely connected.

Customer Complaints

Complaints should not be viewed only as negative events.

They can provide information about:

  • defects
  • service failures
  • process weaknesses
  • unmet expectations

Effective complaint analysis can support improvement.

Service Quality

Quality Management is also important in service organisations.

Service quality may involve:

  • reliability
  • responsiveness
  • assurance
  • empathy
  • physical evidence

Service quality can be difficult to measure because services are often intangible and produced during customer interaction.

Product Quality vs Service Quality

Product Quality Service Quality
Often evaluated through physical characteristics Often evaluated through experience and interaction
Easier to inspect before delivery Often produced and consumed simultaneously
Defects may be physically measurable Service failures may depend on behaviour and timing

Quality Standards

Quality standards help organisations establish consistent procedures and requirements.

Standards may support:

  • process consistency
  • documentation
  • customer confidence
  • quality assurance

ISO and Quality Management Systems

The ISO 9000 family is commonly associated with quality-management principles and systems.

Organisations may use quality-management standards to establish:

  • documented processes
  • responsibilities
  • controls
  • continuous improvement

Students should understand the general purpose of quality-management standards.

Quality Audit

A Quality Audit is a systematic examination of whether quality-related activities and systems follow defined requirements.

Audits may help identify:

  • non-conformities
  • documentation gaps
  • process weaknesses
  • improvement opportunities

Quality Certification

Certification may provide external confirmation that an organisation’s system meets specified standards.

Certification itself does not automatically guarantee that every product is defect-free.

Supplier Quality Management

Supplier quality directly affects the final product or service.

Supplier quality management may involve:

  • supplier selection
  • quality requirements
  • audits
  • incoming quality checks
  • supplier development
  • performance monitoring

Quality at Source

Quality at Source means employees and processes are responsible for preventing defects where the work is performed.

Problems should ideally be corrected immediately rather than passed to the next stage.

Root Cause Analysis

Root Cause Analysis focuses on identifying the underlying cause of a problem rather than only treating its symptoms.

Tools may include:

  • cause-and-effect diagram
  • repeated questioning
  • data analysis

Correct root-cause identification can prevent recurrence.

Five Whys

The Five Whys technique repeatedly asks “Why?” to move from an observed problem toward its underlying cause.

It is simple but useful for many operational problems.

Corrective Action

Corrective action is taken to eliminate the cause of an existing problem.

The objective is to prevent recurrence.

Preventive Action

Preventive action focuses on identifying potential problems before they occur and taking measures to prevent them.

Corrective vs Preventive Action

Corrective Action Preventive Action
Responds to an existing problem Responds to a potential problem
Prevents recurrence Prevents occurrence
Based on detected non-conformity Based on identified risk

Quality Improvement Teams

Cross-functional teams can help solve quality problems involving several departments.

Team members may contribute different expertise and perspectives.

Quality and Productivity

Quality improvement can increase productivity by reducing:

  • rework
  • scrap
  • waiting
  • complaints
  • process failure

Quality and productivity are therefore not necessarily conflicting objectives.

Quality and Cost

Improving quality may require investment in:

  • training
  • prevention
  • technology
  • process improvement

However, these investments can reduce failure costs over time.

The objective is to reduce the total cost of poor quality.

Quality and Competitive Advantage

High quality can support competitive advantage through:

  • customer trust
  • reliability
  • lower cost
  • better reputation
  • differentiation

Quality can therefore be both an operational and strategic issue.

Quality in Manufacturing

Manufacturing quality may involve:

  • materials
  • production processes
  • machine capability
  • inspection
  • specifications
  • reliability

Statistical process methods are often important.

Quality in Services

Service quality may depend heavily on:

  • employee behaviour
  • response time
  • consistency
  • communication
  • customer experience

Quality systems should therefore be adapted to the type of operation.

Quality in Supply Chains

Quality Management connects directly with Supply Chain and Logistics Management (BMB OM 01).

Supply-chain quality depends on:

  • supplier quality
  • handling
  • storage
  • transportation
  • delivery accuracy

A quality problem at one stage may affect the complete supply chain.

Relationship With Business Process Reengineering

Quality Management also connects with Business Process Reengineering (BMB OM 02).

Quality Management often emphasises continuous improvement, while BPR may involve radical redesign when existing processes cannot achieve the required performance.

Both may improve:

  • cost
  • speed
  • customer service
  • productivity

Relationship With Strategic Management

The core subject Strategic Management (BMB301) connects with Quality Management because organisations may use quality as part of strategies based on:

  • differentiation
  • customer satisfaction
  • operational excellence
  • reputation

Quality objectives should therefore align with broader business strategy.

Why Solve AKTU MBA Quality Management PYQs?

Understand the Examination Pattern

Previous-year papers can help students identify whether topics are asked as:

  • definitions
  • short notes
  • comparisons
  • quality tools
  • process-based questions
  • analytical questions
  • case-based applications

Improve Tool-Based Answers

Students should understand when tools such as:

  • Pareto Chart
  • Fishbone Diagram
  • Control Chart
  • Histogram

are used.

Improve Comparison Questions

Important comparisons may include:

  • Quality Control vs Quality Assurance
  • BPR vs TQM
  • Lean vs Six Sigma
  • common cause vs special cause variation
  • corrective vs preventive action

Improve Application-Based Thinking

Students should connect concepts with practical situations such as:

  • reducing defects
  • analysing complaints
  • improving service quality
  • reducing process variation
  • improving supplier quality

Important Topics for Exam Preparation

While practicing AKTU MBA 3rd Sem Quality Management PYQs, students should pay particular attention to:

  • meaning of quality
  • dimensions of quality
  • quality planning
  • quality control
  • quality assurance
  • quality improvement
  • Total Quality Management
  • principles of TQM
  • customer focus
  • continuous improvement
  • Kaizen
  • quality culture
  • Deming
  • Juran
  • Crosby
  • Cost of Quality
  • prevention cost
  • appraisal cost
  • internal failure cost
  • external failure cost
  • seven quality tools
  • Pareto Chart
  • Fishbone Diagram
  • Histogram
  • Control Chart
  • Statistical Quality Control
  • Statistical Process Control
  • process variation
  • process capability
  • acceptance sampling
  • quality circles
  • benchmarking
  • Six Sigma
  • DMAIC
  • Lean
  • Lean Six Sigma
  • 5S
  • Poka-Yoke
  • QFD
  • Voice of Customer
  • ISO quality-management systems
  • quality audits
  • supplier quality
  • root-cause analysis
  • corrective and preventive action

Students should still prepare the complete prescribed syllabus rather than relying only on repeated PYQ topics.

How to Practice Quality Management PYQs

Step 1: Understand the Concept

Study the purpose of each quality concept before memorising definitions.

Step 2: Learn Quality Tools

For every tool, understand:

  • what it is
  • when it is used
  • what information it provides

Step 3: Attempt Related PYQs

Write the answer independently without referring to notes.

Step 4: Use Diagrams Where Appropriate

Simple diagrams can improve answers involving:

  • Fishbone Diagram
  • Pareto analysis
  • control charts
  • DMAIC
  • quality-management process

Step 5: Prepare Comparison Tables

Use tables for concepts that can easily be confused.

Step 6: Connect With Practical Problems

Think about how quality concepts could solve:

  • defects
  • complaints
  • delays
  • variation
  • supplier problems

Step 7: Solve a Complete Paper

After syllabus revision, attempt a full previous-year paper within a fixed time.

This improves:

  • recall
  • answer structure
  • quality terminology
  • application of tools
  • time management

Quick Revision Strategy

For final revision, divide the subject into four broad areas.

Quality Fundamentals

Revise:

  • quality
  • dimensions
  • planning
  • control
  • assurance
  • improvement

TQM and Quality Thinkers

Revise:

  • TQM
  • customer focus
  • Kaizen
  • Deming
  • Juran
  • Crosby
  • Cost of Quality

Quality Tools and Statistical Control

Revise:

  • seven quality tools
  • control charts
  • variation
  • SPC
  • process capability
  • sampling

Modern Quality Approaches

Revise:

  • Six Sigma
  • DMAIC
  • Lean
  • Lean Six Sigma
  • 5S
  • Poka-Yoke
  • benchmarking
  • ISO
  • root-cause analysis

After revision, attempt selected PYQs without referring to your notes.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Quality Management?

Quality Management is an MBA Operation Management specialization subject that focuses on planning, controlling, assuring, and continuously improving the quality of products, services, and organisational processes.

What is the subject code of Quality Management?

The subject code shown for Quality Management is BMB OM 03.

Where can I find AKTU MBA 3rd Sem Quality Management PYQs?

Students can explore AKTU MBA previous-year papers and related academic resources through NotesGallery and use them alongside regular semester preparation.

What is the official website of AKTU?

Students should refer to the AKTU Official Website for official university notices, examination announcements, academic circulars, and authoritative information.

What are the other Operation Management specialization subjects in AKTU MBA 3rd Semester?

The other Operation Management specialization subjects shown are Supply Chain and Logistics Management (BMB OM 01) and Business Process Reengineering (BMB OM 02).

What is the difference between Quality Control and Quality Assurance?

Quality Control focuses mainly on identifying defects through inspection and measurement, while Quality Assurance focuses on designing processes and systems that prevent defects from occurring.

How should I prepare Quality Management using PYQs?

Understand the major quality concepts, learn the purpose of each quality tool, prepare important comparisons, revise TQM and Six Sigma carefully, and solve previous-year questions using practical quality-improvement examples.
